strengths: Addresses an important problem: suppressing unwanted concepts in video generators without expensive retraining. The small exemplar set and closed-form weight edits offer a potentially practical approach.
Table 1 reports substantial reductions across five categories, including gore from 74.9% to 5.3% and pornography from 44.7% to 13.4%. The appendix provides extensive qualitative examples.
The appendix supplies extraction prompts, identifies the edited layers, and derives the weight-fusion formula. Rank and suppression-strength sweeps provide some evidence about parameter sensitivity.
weaknesses: The central cPCA construction has unresolved mathematical problems. For R in R^{H×N}, RᵀR is N×N, not the claimed H×H. More substantively, applying SVD to the indefinite matrix Cr−αCe selects directions by absolute eigenvalue, potentially prioritizing large negative, retain-dominated directions—the opposite of the stated objective. These issues require clarification and corrected experiments.

The claimed subspace dimensionality conflicts with the stated data construction. With five centered difference vectors, the forget covariance has rank at most four; subtracting a positive-semidefinite retain covariance cannot produce 100 positive contrastive directions. The preferred k=100 therefore needs an explanation of additional token/timestep samples or eigenvalue selection. Furthermore, Eq. (8) remains a rank-one correction regardless of k; it does not remove an entire k-dimensional concept subspace.

Comparative evaluation is insufficient to establish the contribution. Results compare only with the unmodified Open-Sora model, without adapted concept-erasure methods or straightforward activation-projection baselines. There are no controlled comparisons of raw refusal vectors, PCA versus cPCA, or text-only versus multimodal extraction, despite the latter being an explicit claimed contribution. Evaluation on one backbone also limits generality.

Preservation of unrelated capabilities is not convincingly demonstrated. There is no broad benign-prompt retention evaluation. The reported FVD uses XCLIP features and compares original unsafe generations with edited generations, rather than validating quality against real videos. Being closer to the original outputs than pure noise is a weak reference point. Small MM-Notox improvements lack uncertainty estimates and do not establish preserved visual quality or temporal coherence.

Safety evaluation is underspecified: sample counts, seeds, confidence intervals, precise GPT-4 version and judging prompts, and frame-to-video aggregation are missing. Independently judging sampled frames is especially inadequate for validating sequential-action safety. Several qualitative examples also exhibit substantial scene or appearance changes, leaving selective suppression versus broader semantic alteration unresolved.

Claims of permanent unlearning, adversarial robustness, and safety 'by construction' exceed the evidence. No adversarial prompting, recovery, or post-edit fine-tuning experiments are provided, and substantial unsafe generation remains. Neither cPCA nor the projection guarantees that benign activations are orthogonal to the refusal vector. The evidence supports behavioral suppression under the tested prompts, not guaranteed removal of the underlying capability.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite useful appendix details. The manuscript does not adequately specify activation sampling and pooling across tokens and diffusion steps, the retain dataset and its size, α, or the construction of paired conditioning images. Some supplied prompt pairs also change multiple attributes simultaneously, such as tiger to kitten and darkness to light, undermining the assumption that their differences isolate only the target concept.

strengths: Addresses an important problem: suppressing unwanted concepts in video generators without expensive retraining. Extracting directions from five multimodal pairs is potentially useful.

Table 1 reports substantial reductions across five categories, including gore from 74.9% to 5.3% and pornography from 44.7% to 13.4%. Qualitative examples provide additional evidence of concept suppression.

The weight-fusion derivation is valid for the stated linear block and avoids additional inference operations. The appendix supplies editing locations and extraction prompts, while the rank and suppression-strength studies offer preliminary ablations.
weaknesses: The central cPCA construction has a substantive mathematical problem. For the indefinite matrix C_r − αC_e, leading singular vectors select directions by absolute eigenvalue, potentially prioritizing large negative, retain-dominated directions. This does not implement the claimed selection of directions with high forget variance and low retain variance; the distinction from leading algebraic eigenvectors needs correction and experimental verification.

The covariance dimensions and sample rank are inconsistent with the reported method. For R ∈ R^(H×N), RᵀR is N×N, not H×H. With five centered difference vectors, the correctly oriented forget covariance has rank at most four, and subtracting a positive-semidefinite retain covariance cannot yield 100 positive contrastive directions. The k=100 interpretation therefore requires an undocumented token/timestep sampling scheme or a different construction.

Evaluation compares only against the original model on one backbone. There are no competing editing or steering baselines and no controlled comparisons against the unrefined refusal vector, ordinary PCA, or text-only extraction. Consequently, neither the benefit of cPCA nor the claimed multimodal advantage is established, and the novelty beyond combining existing steering and cPCA techniques remains insufficiently demonstrated.

Preservation of unrelated capabilities is not convincingly evaluated. Table 2 compares edited unsafe generations with original unsafe generations using XCLIP features, rather than standard FVD features and a real-video reference. Being closer than pure noise is a weak quality criterion. Small MM-Notox improvements do not establish retained capabilities, and there is no quantitative benign-prompt evaluation of quality, temporal coherence, or collateral suppression.

Claims of permanent unlearning, adversarial robustness, and safety 'by construction' exceed the evidence. No adversarial or concept-recovery experiments are reported, and residual unsafe rates reach 33%. Safe inputs are not necessarily orthogonal to the refusal direction, nor does cPCA guarantee semantic isolation. Equation (8) remains a rank-one directional edit regardless of k; removing that component does not prove removal of the underlying concept.

Reproducibility and statistical reporting are incomplete. The manuscript omits the retain-set size and contents, α, precise activation sampling and aggregation, evaluation sample counts, seeds, uncertainty estimates, GPT-4 version, and frame-to-video aggregation rule. Appendix A provides useful layer details but does not resolve these omissions. Frame-based judging also needs validation for sequential-action risks.

The paired examples undermine the assumption that only the target concept changes: Appendix D replaces a tiger with a kitten, darkness with light, and a cable over a cliff with a solid bridge. Such changes introduce semantic confounds. Some qualitative results also show substantial appearance changes or darkening, making selective removal difficult to distinguish from broader degradation.

strengths: Addresses an important problem: targeted concept suppression in video diffusion models without expensive retraining. The small reference set and closed-form weight edits are practically attractive.

Reports substantial reductions in undesirable generations across five categories, including gore from 74.9% to 5.3% and pornography from 44.7% to 13.4%. Supplementary examples provide qualitative evidence of suppression across varied prompts.

Provides an explicit weight-update derivation, reference text prompts, editing locations, and rank/strength sensitivity studies. The limitations acknowledge censorship misuse, reversibility, and single-concept editing.
weaknesses: The central cPCA construction has significant mathematical problems (Section 3.2). For R ∈ R^{H×N}, RᵀR is N×N, not the claimed H×H. More substantively, taking leading singular vectors of the indefinite matrix Cr−αCe selects directions by absolute eigenvalue, potentially prioritizing strongly negative, retain-dominated directions—the opposite of the stated objective. Standard cPCA requires ordering by signed eigenvalues.

The reported rank setting is unexplained under the stated sampling formulation. Five centered difference vectors yield a forget covariance of rank at most four; subtracting a positive-semidefinite retain covariance cannot produce 100 positive contrastive directions. If tokens or diffusion timesteps supply additional observations, that essential construction is missing.

There are no competing-method comparisons: the quantitative tables compare only against the unmodified backbone. Comparisons against direct refusal-vector projection, ordinary PCA, and feasible adaptations of concept-editing approaches are needed to establish the contribution of cPCA. The claimed advantage of multimodal over text-only extraction is not supported by a reported controlled ablation.

Preservation of unrelated capabilities is inadequately evaluated. Table 2 measures distributional distance between unsafe originals and edited outputs, with pure noise as the reference comparison; this does not establish retained quality on benign prompts. The XCLIP-based FVD variant and small MM-Notox improvements lack calibration, uncertainty estimates, and complementary human or temporal-quality evaluation.

Claims of permanent unlearning, adversarial robustness, and safety 'by construction' exceed the evidence. No adversarial evaluation or recovery experiment is reported, and substantial undesirable content remains in several categories. The rank-one projection removes one activation direction, but does not establish removal of the underlying concept or orthogonality to all safe semantics.

Evaluation and reproduction details remain insufficient. The manuscript does not specify per-category evaluation counts, repeated seeds, confidence intervals, the exact GPT-4 evaluator/version and frame-to-video aggregation rule, retain-set composition and size, α, or activation aggregation across tokens and timesteps. The appendix mentions accompanying code, but that resource was not available in the supplied manuscript.

The premise that paired examples differ only in the target concept is violated by several supplied pairs, which also change objects, illumination, and scene structure. Without explicit retention tests, suppression may reflect these confounds rather than selective concept removal. Evaluation on only one backbone further limits the generality of the conclusions.

strengths: Addresses a practically important problem: suppressing unsafe concepts in open-weight video generators without retraining or additional inference overhead. The algebra for absorbing a fixed projection into a subsequent linear layer is sound.

Reports substantial reductions in unsafe generations across two backbones and two benchmarks: 48.9% to 12.6% on Open-Sora/T2VSafetyBench and 68.1% to 9.9% on ZeroScope/SafeSora, with broadly similar aggregate FVD.

Includes useful supplementary experiments covering projection strength, prompt selection, neutral-set resampling, multi-concept removal, motion consistency, and an initial adversarial evaluation. The refusal-only/PCA/cPCA comparison provides some evidence for the refinement.
weaknesses: The central cPCA construction has unresolved mathematical problems. Section 3.2 defines R as H×N but gives RᵀR as an H×H covariance; the same error appears for E. More substantively, selecting leading singular vectors of Cr−αCe ranks eigenvectors by absolute eigenvalue, potentially selecting strongly negative, neutral-dominated directions rather than maximizing contrastive variance. This contradicts the stated objective and requires clarification and corrected experiments.

The reported rank is inconsistent with the stated sampling formulation. With five centered difference vectors, the target covariance has rank at most four; subtracting a positive-semidefinite neutral covariance cannot create additional positive eigenvalues. The selected k=100 therefore cannot represent 100 positive target-enriched directions under the given definitions. If tokens, frames, or timesteps supply additional samples, their construction and aggregation are essential missing details.

Preservation of unrelated capabilities is not established. Most quality and alignment measurements concern unsafe prompts and their sanitized counterparts, rather than a broad held-out benign prompt set. Table 5 evaluates only suppression, so it does not substantiate the claim that cPCA reduces collateral forgetting. The assertion that safe inputs necessarily have zero projection onto the refusal vector is also unsupported.

Baseline comparisons do not establish a convincing safety–utility advantage. Tables 1–2 omit FVD and semantic-alignment results for NullSCE and SAFREE. Table 1 compares averages across different category sets because NullSCE lacks Gore results. The UCE adaptation edits the text encoder rather than its original cross-attention projections, leaving uncertainty about whether the comparison represents a faithful, competitive adaptation.

Reproducibility and evaluation details are insufficient. The paper does not adequately specify activation extraction across diffusion timesteps and spatial/temporal tokens, construction of image-conditioning pairs, benchmark sample counts, random seeds, FVD reference data, alignment encoders, or frame-to-video judgment aggregation. Section 5 selects layers 17–18, whereas Appendix A describes edits in every Open-Sora double block. Main results lack uncertainty estimates and a clearly separated hyperparameter-validation protocol.

Claims of permanent or irreversible unlearning exceed the evidence. A parameter edit establishes persistent intervention, not that a concept is inaccessible through other representations or cannot be recovered. Appendix H's attack test selects 100 prompts already completely suppressed, reports a frame-level outcome rather than the main video-level metric, and provides insufficient attack details or baseline comparisons to establish general robustness.

Efficiency and novelty claims need tighter support. The method combines established difference-of-means directions, contrastive PCA, and linear weight projection; its distinctive contribution is primarily their application to video, while the benefit of joint text/image conditioning is not isolated experimentally. Appendix G requires approximately 1,000 neutral prompts, yet Table 7 describes the cost as ten forward passes and five pairs without accounting clearly for neutral activation collection or hyperparameter search.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: suppressing unsafe concepts in open-weight video generators without costly fine-tuning or additional inference operations.

The reported reductions in unsafe generations are substantial across two backbones and two benchmarks. Tables 1–2 show broadly stable FVD alongside improved safety, providing promising empirical evidence.

The linear weight-fusion derivation is sound for the stated intervention. The appendices provide useful additional experiments on motion consistency, multiple concepts, neutral-set sensitivity, an adapted UCE baseline, and adversarial prompting.
weaknesses: The central cPCA formulation has substantive mathematical problems (Section 3.2). For column-stacked R of shape H×N, RᵀR is N×N, not H×H; the analogous error also affects E, making the stated covariance subtraction dimensionally invalid. More importantly, SVD of the indefinite matrix Cr−αCe selects directions by absolute eigenvalue magnitude, potentially prioritizing strongly negative, neutral-dominated directions. This does not implement the claimed maximization of target variance relative to neutral variance.

The five-pair construction does not explain the reported subspace ranks. Under the stated formulation, the centered target covariance has rank at most four, and subtracting a positive-semidefinite neutral covariance cannot yield more than four positive eigenvalues. The interpretation of k=100 as a target-specific subspace therefore requires clarification. Centering the pair differences also removes their mean—the refusal vector—without establishing that this mean lies in the retained variation subspace.

Claims of permanent, irreversible concept removal and preservation of all unrelated capabilities exceed the evidence. Removing one direction from selected linear maps does not establish that the concept is absent elsewhere in the network. Likewise, safe activations need not be orthogonal to the estimated direction. Appendix H tests only 100 prompts selected for complete pre-attack suppression and reports a frame-level outcome; this offers limited robustness evidence, not a general unlearning guarantee.

The evaluation does not adequately establish selective preservation. FVD and safe-prompt alignment on unsafe-prompt benchmarks are insufficient to measure retained performance on independent benign prompts, especially closely related concepts. Table 5 reports only unsafe-generation rates, so it cannot support the claim that cPCA reduces collateral suppression. A controlled safety–utility comparison, including benign generations and quantitative quality metrics for the ablations, is missing.

Baseline comparisons are incomplete. Tables 1–2 omit FVD and semantic-preservation results for NullSCE and SAFREE, preventing comparison at matched utility. NullSCE's average excludes Gore while the proposed method's average includes it, making the stated average improvement misleading. The UCE adaptation edits the text encoder rather than clearly reproducing its original cross-attention editing mechanism, and Appendix F describes a T2VSafetyBench experiment while reproducing the Sexual-category values from the SafeSora table; the evaluation provenance needs clarification.

Important implementation and evaluation details remain unresolved. Section 5 specifies layers 17–18, whereas Appendix A describes editing every Open-Sora double block. The manuscript does not sufficiently specify activation aggregation across tokens, frames, and diffusion timesteps; construction of image-conditioning pairs; FVD reference data; metric encoders; frame-to-video aggregation; or evaluation sample counts and uncertainty. Although supplementary code is mentioned, these omissions and inconsistencies prevent reproduction from the manuscript.

Novelty and efficiency claims are stronger than demonstrated. The method combines known mean-difference steering, projection-based weight editing, and cPCA; the equations themselves are not specific to temporal generation, and there is no text-only versus joint-conditioning ablation establishing the advertised multimodal contribution. Appendix G requires activations from approximately 1,000 neutral prompts, but Table 7 attributes the method's cost to ten forward passes without clearly accounting for neutral-set construction or hyperparameter selection.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem: suppressing unwanted concepts in open-weight video generators without expensive fine-tuning or additional inference operations.

The reported improvements are substantial across two backbones and two benchmarks: average unsafe-generation rates decrease from 48.9% to 12.6% on Open-Sora and from 68.1% to 9.9% on ZeroScopeT2V, with broadly comparable reported FVD.
The weight-fusion derivation in Equation 8 is valid for a correction immediately preceding a linear map and provides a simple implementation of activation suppression.
The supplementary material adds useful evidence, including comparisons with adapted UCE, neutral-set sensitivity, motion metrics, multi-concept editing, and an initial adversarial-prompt experiment.
weaknesses: The central cPCA construction has unresolved mathematical problems. Section 3.2 defines R as H×N but computes RᵀR and labels it H×H; the same issue affects E. More substantively, selecting the largest singular values of the indefinite matrix Cr−αCe can select strongly negative eigenvalue directions dominated by neutral variance, contrary to the stated contrastive objective. Standard cPCA requires ordering eigenvectors by signed eigenvalues. This is potentially an algorithmic error, not merely notation.

The stated sample construction does not explain the chosen subspace rank. With five centered difference vectors, Cr has rank at most four; subtracting a positive-semidefinite neutral covariance cannot yield more than four positive eigenvalues. The claimed optimum at k=100 therefore needs an explanation of additional token, spatial, or timestep samples, or of why neutral-dominated directions are retained. Moreover, centering removes the mean refusal vector from the covariance calculation without establishing that its projection onto the retained subspace preserves the concept signal.

Implementation details are insufficient and inconsistent. Section 5 specifies layers 17–18, whereas Appendix A describes intervention in every Open-Sora double block. The manuscript does not adequately specify activation pooling, diffusion timesteps, paired-noise handling, image-conditioning construction, or model-specific sampling settings. Appendix G also introduces approximately 1,000 neutral prompts, whose activation-extraction cost is absent from the five-pair, ten-forward-pass efficiency accounting.

Preservation of unrelated capabilities is not convincingly evaluated. FVD and MM-Notox primarily assess outputs from unsafe prompts; there is no broad held-out benign-prompt evaluation demonstrating limited collateral damage. The real-video reference distributions for FVD and the encoders and safe-prompt construction for MM-Notox are unspecified. Table 5 reports suppression alone, so it does not establish that cPCA improves semantic disentanglement or preservation.

Baseline comparisons and evaluation reporting leave important uncertainty. NullSCE and SAFREE lack accompanying quality metrics in the main comparisons, and matched tuning and execution protocols are unclear. Table 1 compares averages over different category sets because NullSCE lacks Gore results. Appendix F labels its UCE experiment as T2VSafetyBench but reproduces the SafeSora Sexual baseline and proposed-method values, leaving its dataset provenance ambiguous. Main results lack uncertainty estimates, clear evaluated sample counts, and a precise frame-to-video aggregation rule.

Claims of permanent, irreversible concept removal and preservation of all unrelated concepts exceed the evidence. A projection absorbed into selected weights establishes a persistent intervention, not removal of the concept throughout the network. The adversarial experiment selects 100 prompts already fully suppressed and reports unsafe-frame rates rather than the main video-level metric; it does not establish general robustness or resistance to recovery.

The methodological novelty is primarily the combination of established activation-direction removal, cPCA, and linear weight fusion. The equations are architecture-agnostic, and the claimed importance of jointly using text and image conditioning is not supported by modality ablations or comparisons isolating temporal information. Stronger evidence is needed to establish a distinctive video-specific contribution.
